I am seventy years old, and I have farmed my land in Quzhou County since I was a young man. I finished middle school, so I can read the instructions on seed bags and fertilizer packs, and I listen to what the agricultural extension station says, but in the end I trust what my own eyes have seen over fifty years. Our land on the North China Plain is flat and the soil is decent, though the groundwater is not what it used to be and the rains come when they please. I have about six mu of good cropland, and I do not see any reason to gamble with strange crops at my age. I will do what I have always done: winter wheat followed by summer maize.

My wheat is already in the ground. I sowed it last October after working the soil with the rotary tiller, using an improved wheat variety—something like Jimai or Luyuan, whatever the county supply shop has that year. Now that spring is starting, I will topdress it with urea when the green-up comes, and again at jointing if the plants look hungry. I give it a good base of compound fertilizer and then supplement with nitrogen two or three times, because around here we have learned that if you do not feed the wheat, it does not feed you. I will irrigate three or four times: the winter irrigation if the soil is dry, the green-up water, the jointing water, and maybe one more at grain filling if the sky gives us nothing. I watch for weeds and aphids, so I usually spray herbicide once and insecticide once or twice; fungicide only if I see spots on the leaves. I expect about 550 kilograms per mu if the weather does not turn cruel.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will plant hybrid maize the same day or the next. Everyone here uses hybrid seed—Denghai or something similar—and you must buy fresh seed every year because saved seed loses its vigor. I will not till the stubble much; I will direct-seed into the wheat residue with the no-till planter. That saves diesel, saves time, and the county technicians say it keeps the moisture in the soil. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing and side-dress urea when the corn is knee-high. Maize needs less water than wheat, so I irrigate twice, once when it is young and once at tasseling if the rains fail. I spray herbicide before the weeds get tall, and insecticide if the corn borers show up. If all goes well, I should get about 580 kilograms per mu of maize. That grain, plus the wheat, is enough for my household and leaves some to sell.
